newsitem.title: PERU: International media sharks descend on Peru.
newsitem.headline: International media sharks descend on Peru.

text.p: The dramatic assault and hostage crisis at the Japanese ambassador's home in Peru was like blood in the water for the international media sharks who have descended on Lima in force, devouring all in their path.
Major television networks from around the globe have jostled each other to secure spots in surrounding buildings to get the all-important shot of the drama unfolding below.

Peru's journalists have also been caught up in the frenzy. Reluctant to give up their front-row view, 10 local reporters have been trapped on a nearby roof since Marxist guerrillas stormed the residence on Tuesday, taking hundreds of hostages.
"We can't leave because the police wouldn't let us back in," local photographer Johnny Laurente shouted down from the two-storey house roof.

As police lines surrounding the property were pushed back, the marooned cameramen could not even come down for supplies, obliging colleagues still on the ground to devise a makeshift pulley to send up food and clothing.
"It's as if we were taken hostage," yelled another.
The story has dominated newspapers, radio and television broadcasts around the world since it broke on Tuesday evening.
Peruvians, many of whom say they are embarassed at being in the world spotlight, have followed every development on live television and radio reports throughout the day.
Peru has taken an unwanted share of media attention this year with two airplane crashes that killed nearly 200 people and a major earthquake.

But the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement assault and hostage drama is by far the biggest story to hit the Andean country since the 1992 capture of Abimael Guzman -- the leader of the rival Maoist Shining Path guerrilla group.
Outside the besieged residence, the constant din of generators hooked up to satellite telephones, camera lights and video equipment, made interviews almost inaudible.
"You walk about 30 feet and it's a zoo," said John Fregener of CNN. Nearby, two pizza delivery boys tried to wake a crumpled reporter who dozed off while waiting for his lunch.
Photographers, cameramen and reporters stood four-deep along the yellow tape police cordon 200 yards (metres) from the residence entrance.

The arrival of somebody to interview can spark fresh rounds of shoving as cameramen cluster around their subject. Those at the back balance precariously on step ladders flailing cameras, tape recorders and microphones.

"All those camermen and journalists almost killed the hostages when they came out," said Danish reporter Anne Sorensern of Friday's release of 38 dazed and stiff captives. "They survived the rebels and then they had to face all this."
Tempers were running high among Japanese journalists travelling with Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, who arrived on Thursday to act as Tokyo's point man in the crisis.

Already frustrated with the tight-lipped diplomacy practised by Ikeda and his entourage, a scuffle erupted after the minister refused to reply to a question from a reporter, who demanded to be treated like "a normal person."

Many of those who rushed to South America when the story broke had only a vague idea of what awaited them. Some, imagining Lima to be high in the Andean mountains, packed lined jackets and sweaters completely unsuitable for the hot summer temperatures in the coastal capital.
"They're much more interesting than the usual guests we get here, I'll miss them," said Rene, a doorman at the swanky Oro Verde hotel, a short cab ride from the action.
